Alegria illustration system for Facebook (Buck)

The illustration and animation system that Buck designed for Facebook from 2017: flat figures built from circles and tubes, with long limbs and blue, violet, or pink skin.

Source
Buck: Facebook Alegria
Creator
Buck, for Facebook
Made

Style

Evidence
Inspected three images from Buck’s project page at 1400 px wide: the cover image of the printed style guide (alegria_thumbnail.png), a hero illustration of figures carrying a thumbs-up, and a spread titled “Figure Construction”. None is stored.

Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

Buck describes the project as “a new style guide, illustration and animation system for the entire Facebook ecosystem” and says Facebook engaged it in 2017. “Alegria is Spanish for ‘joy’.” Buck.

Buck credits Xoana Herrera as design lead, Amelia Giller and Janice Ahn as senior art directors, and ten core illustrators. The library also covers transport, plants, animals, buildings, and hands. Buck.

AIGA Eye on Design (21 August 2019) treats Alegria as the model for the tech illustration style and quotes Herrera on “ethnically non-specific” characters. AIGA Eye on Design.

Observed

  • In the hero illustration, six figures in flat fills carry a large blue thumbs-up. Arms and legs are long tubes that bend in smooth curves; one figure rides a unicycle.
  • Skin is violet, pink, pale blue, green, and yellow. Hair and some trousers are near-black navy.
  • Heads are small in relation to the bodies, and faces have only dots and short lines.
  • Some limbs carry a fine speckled grain in one tone, and a few details use thin colored lines.
  • A style-guide spread titled “Figure Construction” says the figures are “11 1/2 heads tall”, that “limbs are composed of cylindrical shapes”, and that men’s arms reach the knee.
  • Other guide pages show a woman with blue skin holding up a cup, a dog and fruit built from circles, and a rule on how to crop tall figures at the frame edge.

Why it belongs

The construction rules (heads as circles, limbs as cylinders, 11½ heads tall) explain why the style spread so fast: any illustrator can follow them and the results match.

The grain on some limbs shows that the original system allowed a little texture. Many later imitations removed it and kept only flat fills.

Borrow

Build figures to a fixed head count (about 11 heads tall) with cylinder limbs, so a team of illustrators produces matching people.

Give each scene one oversized object that the figures lift or carry together.
